query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticles that preserve their structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions do so because a high configurational entropy together with associated severe lattice distortions induces local atomic diffusion barriers that suppress phase segregation and elemental leaching.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized by a controlled, one‐pot colloidal or laser-based method, exhibiting homogeneous atomic mixing and high configurational disorder.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled post-synthesis heat treatment (annealing) at an intermediate temperature for a defined time to promote slight local chemical ordering without triggering overall phase segregation, compared to a baseline rapid quench condition.
generation.conditions: Service temperatures in the range of 773–1173 K for catalytic reactions and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications, where atomic mobility is elevated but can be modulated by local energy barriers.
generation.structural_mediator: The local atomic ordering (or alternatively its absence) that modulates lattice distortions and diffusion barriers.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in the as-synthesized nanoparticles creates extensive chemical disorder and severe lattice distortions. This increases local energy barriers for atomic rearrangements, thus hindering diffusional processes that would otherwise lead to phase separation or elemental segregation under high-temperature operation. A mild annealing that slightly enhances local ordering (without precipitating a full phase change) tests whether a controlled degree of short-range order can further pin the structure versus the baseline disordered state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles subjected to the tailored heat treatment (intervention) will exhibit enhanced stability during high-temperature operation (evidenced by minimal grain growth, retention of homogeneous elemental distribution, and stable catalytic performance) relative to rapidly cooled nanoparticles, which may show more gradual phase separation or compositional drift.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced by rapid quenching that retain a purely disordered, high entropy state without induced local ordering.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is specifically applicable to multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles operating under moderately high (773–1173 K) and extended temperature regimes (up to 1923 K in thermoelectric applications) where atomic diffusion is activated but can be counteracted by intrinsic energy barriers. It may not apply if synthesis conditions or elemental combinations lead to intrinsic immiscibility regardless of entropy effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise contribution of local chemical ordering versus pure configurational entropy in establishing sufficient diffusion barriers is not fully quantified, and the optimal heat treatment parameters remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles: one set is rapidly quenched to retain maximum configurational disorder, and the other undergoes a controlled annealing step to induce partial local ordering. Subject both sets to accelerated aging tests at a service-relevant temperature (e.g., 1000 K) for extended durations. Characterize the structure (using XRD, TEM, and EDS mapping) and monitor catalytic (or thermoelectric) performance over time.
measurements: Grain size and phase purity via XRD
Elemental distribution homogeneity and presence of secondary phases via TEM and EDS
Performance metrics (e.g., catalytic activity or thermoelectric efficiency) before and after aging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the annealed and rapidly quenched nanoparticles exhibit statistically indistinguishable structural and performance degradation during high-temperature service, or if the anticipated enhancement in stability for the annealed samples is not observed, then the hypothesis that local ordering (mediated by controlled annealing) significantly contributes to stabilizing the nanoparticles beyond the effect of configurational entropy would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Our results provide fresh insights into the design and property tailoring of emerging classes of HEOs. However, the oxygen chemical potential, μO, exerts a profound influence on the phase stability of Mn2O3 and Fe2O3 compared to that of MnO and FeO. This μO can be tuned by controlling experimental variables such as temperature, T, and oxygen partial pressure, PO2. Recently, we demonstrated that the consideration of PO2 in our calculations was necessary for understanding the formability of entropy stabilized pyrochlore structures (). In this work, we estimate the phase stability of Fe- and Mn-containing oxides in relation to their stable forms, as a function of T and PO2. The formation abilities of FCOs containing Mn and Fe are re-evaluated using MnO and FeO as the reference oxides. These formation abilities will be valid under the experimental conditions where MnO and FeO are more stable than Mn2O3 and Fe2O3. We find that the formation abilities of FCOs containing Mn and Fe are markedly different, compliant with the stability of their reference oxides. Therefore, we predict that several different HEOs can potentially be synthesized in pure rocksalt structures under low oxygen partial pressure.

In the era of nanotechnology, the art of manipulating metals at the atomic scale has proven to be essential for the development of advanced nanoscale materials. The fabrication of semiconductor chips, nowadays essential for computing, communication, or transportation systems, is probably one of the most paradigmatic examples. Noble metals have drawn significant interest due to their high chemical stability, even in the nanoscale, where most metals tend to rust and oxidize., Moreover, they are critical for the fabrication of nanostructures that are crucial to face challenges such as climate change commitments.− Platinum, palladium, or iridium nanoparticles, and many of their alloys, are among the most active materials for the (electro)catalytic production of hydrogen, the element with the greatest potential to replace fossil fuels in energy storage, transportation, and use.− In medicine, the strong optical characteristics of gold nanoparticles can be applied to develop sensors for early detection of various diseases, diagnoses, or cancer treatments.,, Nevertheless, obtaining valuable material from metals depends on our ability to transform them into nano-objects with defined shapes,
